description: Prohibited substances, blood doping and the advantages and disadvantages for performers.
content_html:
Performance-Enhancing Drugs in Sport

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances that athletes take to improve their physical or psychological output in training or competition. Most PEDs are prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and the governing bodies of individual sports. The use of prohibited substances is considered cheating because it undermines the principle of fair competition and often poses serious health risks to the performer. Despite this, doping remains a persistent problem across numerous sports at elite level. Understanding which categories of PED exist, why performers use them and the consequences they carry is essential both for the exam and for understanding the ethical landscape of modern sport.

Stimulants

Stimulants are substances that increase alertness, reduce the sensation of fatigue and heighten aggression and competitiveness. They can improve reaction time and allow a performer to sustain high-intensity effort for longer. Sports such as sprint cycling or combat sports, where aggression and alertness are direct performance assets, have seen stimulant abuse. Side effects include elevated heart rate, anxiety, insomnia and in severe cases heart attack. Stimulants are banned in competition by most governing bodies.

Narcotic Analgesics

Narcotic analgesics are powerful painkillers that reduce or eliminate the sensation of pain. Performers who have sustained injuries, or who train at a very high volume (which inevitably produces chronic discomfort), may be tempted to use narcotic analgesics to continue competing. The critical danger is that pain is the body’s warning signal. A performer who cannot feel pain is at serious risk of worsening an existing injury, potentially causing long-term damage to tendons, ligaments or bones. Side effects include dependency, nausea and loss of coordination.

Anabolic Agents

Anabolic agents, commonly called anabolic steroids, are synthetic hormones that accelerate the development of muscle mass and reduce recovery time between training sessions. They are most commonly associated with power-based sports such as weightlifting, shot put or rugby, where muscle mass is a direct determinant of performance. By allowing performers to train harder and recover faster, anabolic agents provide a substantial competitive advantage. Side effects include liver damage, cardiovascular disease, hormonal disruption (including in secondary sexual characteristics) and, in adolescent users, premature closure of growth plates, which can permanently reduce height.

Key Fact

Five main categories of prohibited substance: stimulants (alertness, reduce fatigue — sprint/combat sports); narcotic analgesics (mask pain — injury management); anabolic agents (muscle mass — power sports); diuretics (weight loss — weight-category sports); peptide hormones such as EPO (oxygen-carrying capacity — endurance sports).

Diuretics

Diuretics accelerate fluid loss through urine production. In weight-category sports such as boxing, judo or weightlifting, an athlete might use a diuretic in the days before weigh-in to shed enough fluid to compete in a lower weight category, gaining a size and strength advantage against smaller opponents. Diuretics are also sometimes misused to dilute urine samples, reducing the concentration of other banned substances and making them harder to detect. Side effects include dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, muscle cramps and, in severe cases, cardiac arrhythmia.

Peptide Hormones and EPO

Erythropoietin (EPO) is the most widely known peptide hormone misused in sport. Normally produced naturally by the kidneys in response to low oxygen levels (such as at altitude), EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells. More red blood cells means a greater capacity to carry oxygen to working muscles, which directly improves aerobic endurance performance. EPO has been widely associated with endurance cycling, cross-country skiing and distance running. Side effects include dangerous thickening of the blood (increased viscosity), which slows blood flow and increases the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart attack — particularly during sleep, when heart rate is low and blood flows slowly.

Blood doping achieves the same outcome as EPO — increased red blood cell count — through a different mechanism. An athlete removes a quantity of their own blood several weeks before competition. The body naturally replaces it. The stored blood is then frozen and re-infused just before the competition begins, producing an artificially elevated red blood cell count and enhanced oxygen-carrying capacity. The benefits are the same as EPO: improved aerobic endurance performance. The side effects are significant: the blood thickens after re-infusion (increased viscosity), which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. There is also a serious risk of infection from contaminated equipment and the risk of an embolism (a blockage of a blood vessel by a clot or air bubble), which can be fatal.

Beta Blockers

Beta blockers are a distinct category of substance that are permitted in most sports but are restricted in a small number where fine motor control is critical to performance. They reduce heart rate, lower muscle tension and decrease blood pressure by blocking the effects of adrenaline. In sports requiring extreme precision — such as archery, shooting or snooker — a reduced heart rate and steadier hand provides a direct performance advantage. Side effects include nausea, weakness and potentially dangerous cardiac problems. Beta blockers should only be used under medical prescription; athletes using them without medical need in restricted sports face sanctions.

Key Fact

Blood doping and EPO both increase red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity. Both cause dangerous thickening of the blood (increased viscosity), raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism. Blood doping additionally carries risks of infection and embolism from the transfusion process.

Advantages and Disadvantages for Performers

The spec requires students to evaluate both sides of PED use from the performer’s perspective. The potential advantages include: an increased chance of winning; access to fame and financial rewards that success brings; and, where many competitors are doping, a perceived level playing field. The disadvantages are substantial and wide-ranging. Health risks range from liver damage to cardiac arrest and addiction. Detection leads to bans, fines and career destruction. Reputational damage can be permanent and extends to sponsors, national associations and fellow competitors who competed cleanly. For sport as a whole, high-profile doping scandals damage credibility and can reduce spectator interest and commercial revenue over time.

Some athletes have argued that if everyone is doping, using PEDs simply restores a level playing field. Students should be able to challenge this reasoning. First, not all athletes dope — those who refuse to do so are placed at a systematic disadvantage, which is not a level playing field. Second, access to the most effective and safest doping protocols depends on resources, meaning wealthier athletes and nations dope more safely and effectively than poorer ones — an inequality within the inequality. Third, the argument normalises a race to ever-higher levels of doping that accelerates health risks for all. A strong 9-mark answer will recognise the argument, acknowledge why it holds superficial appeal to performers, and then dismantle it with these counter-points.
exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question about a specific PED category, give three distinct pieces of information: what the substance does, which type of performer might use it and why, and one side effect. Avoid the common error of repeating the same point in different words — for example, “it increases muscle mass” and “it helps muscles grow” are the same point and will only earn 1 mark. For a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question on whether PED use can ever be justified, you must present genuine arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion. A response that only condemns PED use without engaging with the arguments athletes make for using them will be capped at the Developing band. Use the ‘For X… However Y…’ structure with a specific sporting type anchored to each side.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five prohibited categories: stimulants (alertness), narcotic analgesics (pain), anabolic agents (muscle mass), diuretics (weight loss), peptide hormones including EPO (oxygen-carrying capacity). Blood doping achieves the same effect as EPO via transfusion. Beta blockers are restricted, not banned outright.
  • EPO and blood doping both thicken the blood (increased viscosity), raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism — potentially fatal side effects that apply to both methods.
  • Advantages for performers include potential success, fame and wealth; disadvantages include severe health risks, bans, fines, reputational damage and long-term career destruction.

practice_questions.text: Identify the category of performance-enhancing drug most likely to be used by a powerlifter who wants to increase muscle mass rapidly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anabolic agents (1) or anabolic steroids (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'blood doping' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that blood doping involves removing and re-infusing blood to increase red blood cell count; 1 mark for linking this to an improvement in oxygen-carrying capacity or endurance performance. Example full-mark answer: 'Blood doping is a prohibited method in which an athlete removes a quantity of their own blood weeks before competition, stores it, and re-infuses it just before competing in order to artificially increase red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the effects and side effects of using EPO as a performance-enhancing substance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that EPO increases red blood cell production; 1 mark for explaining that this increases oxygen-carrying capacity and benefits endurance performance; 1 mark for a valid side effect (blood thickening/increased viscosity; risk of heart attack or stroke; risk of blood clot/embolism). Example full-mark answer: 'EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells in the body (1). More red blood cells increase the blood’s ability to carry oxygen to working muscles, improving aerobic endurance performance (1). A dangerous side effect is that EPO thickens the blood, increasing viscosity, which can lead to blood clots, heart attack or stroke (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a performer might choose to use anabolic agents, and two reasons why this decision could have serious negative consequences for them.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 reasons for + 2 consequences): must cover both sides for full marks.
Reasons for using (up to 2 marks): increased muscle mass improving strength and power performance (1); faster recovery from training enabling greater training volume (1); increased chance of competition success leading to financial reward and recognition (1).
Negative consequences (up to 2 marks): risk of liver damage and cardiovascular disease (1); hormonal disruption, including in secondary sexual characteristics (1); risk of ban, fine and permanent reputational damage if detected (1); permanent growth plate damage in adolescent users (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level distance runner has been told by a teammate that EPO is undetectable and that many top competitors use it anyway. Evaluate the arguments for and against the runner using EPO, and reach a conclusion about whether such arguments can be justified.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting genuine arguments on both sides. Challenges the ‘level playing field’ reasoning with counter-arguments. Uses accurate physiological vocabulary (red blood cells, oxygen-carrying capacity, viscosity). Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Consistent sporting application throughout.
Secure: Covers arguments for and against EPO use; mostly accurate physiological understanding; mostly applied to an endurance sporting context; generally balanced.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or acknowledges both sides without developing either; some relevant points but underdeveloped; limited sporting application.
Emerging: Basic statements that EPO is wrong or helpful without physiological explanation; no balanced argument; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable arguments for using EPO: increased red blood cells improve oxygen delivery to muscles, directly improving endurance performance; may be perceived as levelling the field if others are doping; potential for greater competition success, fame and financial reward; if truly undetectable, perceived risk of sanction is low.
Arguments against using EPO: blood thickening significantly raises risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism — particularly dangerous during sleep when heart rate is low; the ‘level playing field’ argument is flawed because many competitors do not dope; wealthier competitors access safer protocols creating new inequalities; if detected, consequences include lengthy ban, loss of results, fines and career-ending reputational damage; the use violates the contract to compete and the ethical foundations of sport; the sport of distance running suffers credibility damage from doping scandals, reducing sponsorship and audience engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two side effects of blood doping for a performer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct side effects, or 1 mark for identifying the mechanism and 1 mark for explaining the consequence. Acceptable side effects: thickening of blood/increased viscosity (1); risk of heart attack (1); risk of stroke/embolism/blockage of a blood vessel (1); potential infection from contaminated equipment (1); risk from the transfusion process itself (1). Example 3-mark answer: 'Blood doping causes the blood to thicken as red blood cell count increases (1). This increased viscosity slows blood flow and raises the risk of a heart attack (1). There is also a risk of embolism — a blockage of a blood vessel — which can be fatal (1).'

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of performer would most likely misuse diuretics as a performance-enhancing strategy?
options: A marathon runner seeking to improve endurance
A boxer trying to lose weight before a weigh-in
A shot-putter seeking to increase muscle mass
An archer seeking steadier fine motor control

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a side effect shared by both EPO use and blood doping?
options: Increased blood viscosity raising risk of heart attack

knowledge_checks.q: EPO and blood doping both increase red blood cell count, which improves the blood's ability to carry _____ to working muscles.
Narcotic analgesics are painkilling drugs that mask pain, making them dangerous because pain is the body's natural _____ signal.
Match each PED category to the type of performer most likely to use it:
right: Power athletes seeking rapid muscle growth (e.g. weightlifters)
Sprint or combat sport athletes seeking alertness and reduced fatigue
Precision sport performers requiring steady fine motor control (e.g. archers)

flashcard_questions.a: Substances taken by performers to gain an advantage, most of which are prohibited in sport.

flashcard_questions.q: What do stimulants do for a performer?
flashcard_questions.a: Increase alertness, reduce fatigue and heighten competitiveness and aggression.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are narcotic analgesics dangerous in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: They mask pain — the body's warning signal — risking worsening of existing injuries.
Promote muscle growth and increase lean body mass, accelerating strength training adaptations.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a boxer use diuretics?
flashcard_questions.a: To lose weight rapidly before a weigh-in and compete in a lower weight category.

flashcard_questions.q: What does EPO do in the body?
flashcard_questions.a: Stimulates red blood cell production, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of performer benefits most from EPO?
flashcard_questions.a: Endurance performers such as distance runners or cyclists.
Removing, storing and re-infusing blood before competition to increase red blood cell count.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the shared dangerous side effect of EPO and blood doping?
flashcard_questions.a: Increased blood viscosity, meaning the blood thickens and flows more slowly around the body.

flashcard_questions.q: What do beta blockers do for performers?
flashcard_questions.a: Reduce heart rate, muscle tension and blood pressure, improving precision and fine motor control.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one sport where beta blockers are restricted.
flashcard_questions.a: Archery, shooting or snooker — any sport requiring fine motor control and precision.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two disadvantages of using PEDs for a performer.
flashcard_questions.a: Risk of serious health side effects; potential ban, fine and career-ending reputational damage.

glossary_terms.definition: Substances taken by performers to gain an advantage in competition or training, most of which are prohibited by sporting governing bodies.
Drugs that increase alertness, reduce fatigue and heighten competitiveness, prohibited in most sports during competition.
Painkilling drugs that mask the sensation of pain, allowing performers to train or compete through injuries that would otherwise prevent participation.
Synthetic hormones that promote muscle growth and increase lean body mass, used illegally by power and strength athletes to accelerate training adaptations.
Substances that increase the rate of urine production, used to achieve rapid weight loss in weight-category sports or to dilute the concentration of other prohibited substances.

A naturally occurring hormone produced by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production; synthetic EPO is a prohibited peptide hormone used to boost oxygen-carrying capacity in endurance athletes.
A prohibited method in which an athlete removes, stores and later re-infuses their own blood to increase red blood cell count before competition.
